unitTitle: The Bengal School and Cultural Nationalism
topicTitle: Abanindranath Tagore, Nandalal Bose, Jamini Roy, National Flag Symbolism

ncertReference.book: An Introduction to Indian Art - Part II (Class XII)
ncertReference.chapter: Chapter 3: The Bengal School and Cultural Nationalism

thirtySecondSummary: The Bengal School of Art arose during the Swadeshi Movement (early 20th c.) led by Abanindranath Tagore and E.B. Havell, rebelling against colonial British academic realism (Raja Ravi Varma's Western oil aesthetic) to resurrect an authentic Pan-Asian and indigenous Indian artistic identity.

Abanindranath Tagore developed the unique Japanese 'Wash Technique' (learned from Okakura Kakuzo, Yokoyama Taikan, and Hishida Shunso), creating misty, dreamlike, evocative spiritual moods (masterpiece: 'Bharat Mata', 1905).

Nandalal Bose, principal of Kala Bhavana (Visva-Bharati, Santiniketan), grounded modern Indian art in folk vitality, rural Indian life, and monumental public murals (e.g., Haripura Congress posters, 'Siva and Sati', 'Tiller of the Soil').

Jamini Roy rejected academic realism and nostalgic wash romanticism to adopt the flat, vigorous, linear folk idiom of Bengal's rural Kalighat patuas, using earth colors on woven khadi (e.g., 'Three Pujarins', 'Mother and Child').

The Evolution of the Indian National Flag (1906 Calcutta flag -> 1921 Pingali Venkayya Swaraj flag -> 1947 Tiranga designed by Surayya Tyabji / Badruddin Tyabji committee) embodies national unity, courage, peace, fertility, and the 24-spoke Ashoka Dharma Chakra.

coreConcepts.title: Ideological Genesis of the Bengal School: Swadeshi Art
coreConcepts.explanation: Under colonial rule, British Art Schools (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras) imposed rigid Victorian academic realism and Greco-Roman plaster cast copying, denigrating Indian art as lacking perspective and anatomy. In response, E.B. Havell (Principal of Government School of Art, Calcutta) and Abanindranath Tagore spearheaded an artistic revolution. They drew inspiration from Ajanta and Bagh murals, Mughal and Rajput miniatures, and Japanese wash painting. They founded the 'Indian Society of Oriental Art' (1907). Art was viewed as a sacred nationalist tool to awaken the spiritual consciousness of colonized India.
keyTakeaways: Rebellion against European academic realism and British colonial art pedagogy.
E.B. Havell & Abanindranath Tagore: Key intellectual architects of Swadeshi art.
Inspirations: Ajanta frescoes, Mughal miniatures, Japanese wash techniques.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 3, Section 'Origin and Development of Bengal School', pp. 70-76.

coreConcepts.title: Master Artists of the Movement
coreConcepts.explanation:
1. Abanindranath Tagore (1871-1951): Pioneer of the Wash technique. In 'Bharat Mata' (1905), he visualized the motherland not as a fearsome goddess with weapons, but as a serene four-armed ascetic maiden (Brahmo-Vaishnavite icon) holding four Swadeshi boons: Book (Veda/Education), Sheaf of Paddy (Food/Annam), White Cloth (Vastra/Clothing), and Rosary Beads (Japamala/Spiritual Wisdom).
2. Nandalal Bose (1882-1966): Known as 'Master Moshai'. In 1937-38, Mahatma Gandhi invited him to decorate the Haripura Congress session; Bose created the famous 'Haripura Posters' portraying Indian peasants, carpenters, drummers, and 'Tiller of the Soil' with vigorous tempera brushwork. He also illuminated the original manuscript of the Constitution of India.
3. Jamini Roy (1887-1972): Trained academically, Roy boldly renounced Western oil painting to revive the bold, sweeping lines and vibrant earth pigments of rural Bengal's Kalighat pats. His figures feature large almond eyes, flat color blocks, and profound folk dignity (e.g., 'Three Pujarins', 'Gopini with Milk Bowl').
4. Asit Kumar Haldar, Kshitindranath Majumdar, and Sarada Ukil spread the Bengal School across India (Lucknow, Allahabad, Delhi).
keyTakeaways: Bharat Mata (1905, Abanindranath): 4 boons = Food, Clothing, Education, Spiritual Salvation.
Nandalal Bose: Haripura Posters (Tiller of the Soil), illuminated the Indian Constitution.
Jamini Roy: Kalighat folk revival, natural pigments (clay, turmeric, soot, vermilion).

coreConcepts.title: Evolution and Symbolism of the Indian National Flag
coreConcepts.explanation:
The Indian National Flag evolved through three canonical historical milestones:
1. 1906 (Calcutta / Parsi Bagan Flag): Unfurled on August 7, 1906. Three horizontal stripes: Green (top with 8 lotuses for 8 provinces), Yellow (middle with 'Vande Mataram' in Devanagari), and Red (bottom with a sun and crescent moon).
2. 1921 (Swaraj Flag, Vijayawada): Designed by Pingali Venkayya and presented to Mahatma Gandhi. Two colors (Red for Hindus, Green for Muslims); Gandhi added a White stripe at the top for other minorities and a spinning wheel (Charkha) symbolizing economic self-reliance.
3. 1947 (The Tiranga): Adopted on July 22, 1947 by the Constituent Assembly. Ratio 3:2. Top stripe Deep Saffron (Kesari) represents courage and self-sacrifice; Middle White stripe represents peace, truth, and purity; Bottom Dark Green stripe represents faith, chivalry, and agricultural prosperity. The spinning wheel was replaced by the 24-spoke navy-blue Ashoka Dharma Chakra from the Sarnath Lion Capital, signifying eternal cosmic law and righteous progress.
keyTakeaways: Ashoka Chakra: Navy blue, 24 spokes, Sarnath Lion Capital origin, symbolizes 24 hours of ceaseless righteous action.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 3, Section 'The National Flag of India', pp. 92-97.

keyFacts.formulaOrFact: Painting dipped repeatedly in water after layers of watercolor wash, producing soft diffused contours
keyFacts.explanation: Introduced by Abanindranath Tagore after interacting with Japanese artists Yokoyama Taikan and Hishida Shunso in Calcutta.
keyFacts.examTip: CUET asks which Japanese artists influenced Abanindranath's wash method.

keyFacts.formulaOrFact: Artist: Abanindranath Tagore | Medium: Watercolor Wash on paper
keyFacts.explanation: Depicts motherland as an ascetic clad in saffron, holding Shikhya (book), Dikshya (rosary), Anna (paddy), and Vastra (cloth).
keyFacts.examTip: Sister Nivedita hailed it as the supreme iconic embodiment of Swadeshi spiritual nationalism.

keyFacts.formulaOrFact: Artist: Nandalal Bose | Medium: Poster paint / Tempera on handmade paper
keyFacts.explanation: Decorated the pandal of the INC Session at Haripura at Gandhiji's request, celebrating common rural working-class Indians.
keyFacts.examTip: Masterpiece from this series: 'Tiller of the Soil' (Indian farmer ploughing with bullocks).

keyFacts.formulaOrFact: Artist: Jamini Roy | Style: Bengal Folk / Kalighat idiom | Medium: Tempera
keyFacts.explanation: Three dignified women holding ceremonial offerings; defined by bold sweeping black outlines, large almond eyes, and flat indigo/yellow tones.
keyFacts.examTip: Jamini Roy received Padma Bhushan (1955) and is declared an Indian National Art Treasure.

workedExamples.question: In Abanindranath Tagore's iconic 1905 painting 'Bharat Mata', what four symbolic objects are held in the four hands of the maiden deity?

options.text: Book (Veda), Sheaf of Paddy, Piece of White Cloth, and Rosary (Japamala)
Bow, Arrow, Plow, and Spinning Wheel

solutionSteps: Step 1: Recall the ideological meaning of 'Bharat Mata' by Abanindranath Tagore created during the Swadeshi anti-partition movement.
Step 2: Abanindranath broke away from militant imagery, portraying the nation as an ascetic mother providing four basic human blessings (Shiksha, Anna, Vastra, and Diksha).
Step 3: These correspond to: Book (Veda), Paddy sheaf, White cloth, and Akshamala (Rosary).
workedExamples.cuetInsight: The four objects in Bharat Mata's hands are among the most frequently tested visual analysis questions in CUET.

workedExamples.question: Which legendary Indian modern master was tasked with decorating the pandals of the 1937 Haripura Congress session by Mahatma Gandhi?
solutionSteps: Step 1: Identify the context: Haripura Congress session (1937) and Mahatma Gandhi's personal invitation.
Step 2: Nandalal Bose ('Master Moshai'), Principal of Kala Bhavana, Santiniketan, was commissioned to create indigenous public art.
Step 3: He created the celebrated 'Haripura Posters' depicting daily village life.
workedExamples.cuetInsight: Nandalal Bose's association with Gandhiji and the Haripura Posters ('Tiller of the Soil') is a staple question.

howCuetAsks.typicalStem: The 24 spokes of the Ashoka Dharma Chakra in the Indian National Flag represent what, and when was the flag officially adopted?
howCuetAsks.strategy: Memorize: Adopted July 22, 1947; Ratio 3:2; 24 spokes represent 24 hours of moral progress derived from Sarnath Lion Capital.

howCuetAsks.patternType: Artist Philosophy: Jamini Roy vs. Abanindranath
howCuetAsks.typicalStem: Why did Jamini Roy reject European academic oil painting in favor of Kalighat patua folk art?
howCuetAsks.strategy: Focus on Roy's quest for an art accessible to the common masses using local materials (earthen pigments on khadi).

commonTraps.trap: Confusing who painted 'Journey's End' vs. 'Tiller of the Soil'.
commonTraps.whyItTraps: Both are celebrated Bengal School works. 'Journey's End' (collapsing camel under twilight) was painted by Abanindranath Tagore; 'Tiller of the Soil' (Haripura poster) was painted by Nandalal Bose.

quickRevisionCard.title: Bengal School & National Flag Summary

Technique: Wash method (Japanese influence of Okakura, Taikan, Shunso) + Ajanta/Mughal aesthetics.
Abanindranath: 'Bharat Mata' (1905), 'Journey's End'; spiritual contemplative wash.
Nandalal Bose: 'Master Moshai', Santiniketan; Haripura Posters ('Tiller of the Soil'), Constitution illustration.
Jamini Roy: Kalighat patua folk revival, bold fluid black lines, tempera on khadi ('Three Pujarins').
National Flag: Adopted 22 July 1947; Ratio 3:2; Saffron, White, Green; 24-spoke Navy Blue Ashoka Chakra from Sarnath.

practiceQuestions.question: Who was the English principal of the Government Art School, Calcutta, who assisted Abanindranath Tagore in spearheading the Bengal School movement?
practiceQuestions.explanation: E.B. Havell played a foundational role by removing European plaster casts and encouraging students to study Ajanta murals and Indian miniature traditions.

practiceQuestions.question: In Nandalal Bose's famous Haripura Congress poster 'Tiller of the Soil', what medium and surface were utilized?

options.text: Tempera / poster color on handmade paper

practiceQuestions.explanation: Nandalal Bose used quick, bold tempera brushwork on locally produced handmade mill-board paper to produce dozens of posters depicting everyday rural occupations.

practiceQuestions.question: The iconic painting 'Journey's End' depicting a collapsed, exhausted camel against a twilight sky laden with heavy burdens was created by:
practiceQuestions.explanation: 'Journey's End' is an emotive wash masterpiece by Abanindranath Tagore (1913), allegorically representing the relentless exploitation and burden borne by silent working creatures.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the official statutory dimensional ratio of the length to width of the Indian National Flag?
practiceQuestions.explanation: According to the Flag Code of India and the Constituent Assembly resolution, the ratio of the length to the height (width) of the flag is 3:2.

practiceQuestions.question:
Given below are two statements:
Assertion (A): Jamini Roy renounced Western oil paints to adopt indigenous organic and mineral pigments like yellow ochre, vermilion, soot, and chalk.
Reason (R): He wanted his art to be rooted in the visual language of rural folk patuas and accessible to everyday Indian society.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)

practiceQuestions.explanation: Both statements are completely true and (R) precisely articulates Jamini Roy's artistic mission of democratizing art via Kalighat folk traditions.

practiceQuestions.question: On which historic date did the Constituent Assembly officially adopt the Tiranga as Independent India's National Flag?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The National Flag of India was adopted in its present form during an ad-hoc Constituent Assembly meeting held on 22 July 1947, shortly before Independence.

practiceQuestions.question: The Navy Blue wheel (Dharma Chakra) in the center of the National Flag was taken from the abacus of which ancient Indian monument?

options.text: Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath

practiceQuestions.explanation: The 24-spoke Dharma Chakra was adopted from the abacus of the 3rd century BCE Lion Capital of Emperor Ashoka at Sarnath.

practiceQuestions.question:
Match List-I (Artwork) with List-II (Master Artist):
List-I:
(P) Bharat Mata
(Q) Siva and Sati
(R) Three Pujarins
(S) Rasa-Lila

List-II:
(1) Jamini Roy
(2) Nandalal Bose
(3) Abanindranath Tagore
(4) Kshitindranath Majumdar
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bharat Mata is by Abanindranath Tagore; Siva and Sati is by Nandalal Bose; Three Pujarins is by Jamini Roy; Rasa-Lila is by Kshitindranath Majumdar.

practiceQuestions.question: The Indian Society of Oriental Art was established in Calcutta in which year to nurture Swadeshi art and award scholarships?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Indian Society of Oriental Art was founded in 1907 in Calcutta by Abanindranath Tagore and brother Gaganendranath Tagore along with sympathizers like Sir John Woodroffe.

practiceQuestions.question: Who designed the original Swaraj flag featuring Red and Green bands with a Charkha, presented to Mahatma Gandhi at Vijayawada in 1921?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pingali Venkayya designed the 1921 Swaraj flag and presented it to Mahatma Gandhi during the All India Congress Committee session at Vijayawada.
